crime.value: Murder by gunshot of a blackmailer at a private estate's old carriage house; the central question is not whodunit but what happened to the concealed body — where did it go after being moved?
crime.quote: I had also been able to hear the muffled report which had abruptly terminated their conversation.

victim.value: A small, sharp-featured blackmailer extorting Uncle Walter over his affairs with show girls; killable because he demanded more money and foolishly agreed to a late-night meeting on the killer's own property
victim.quote: a criminal, naturally. In his case, a blackmailer—and not at all a clever or cautious one

closed_world.value: A small private estate with only four residents — Harold, Uncle Walter, Aunt Pearl, and Elsie the maid — plus its grounds, carriage house, hedges and adjoining creek/grove
closed_world.quote: She was also the only person who lived on this small estate except for myself. Uncle Walter, and Aunt Pearl.

culprit_and_motive.value: Uncle Walter, a pompous, tightfisted lawyer, shot the extortionist to stop escalating blackmail demands over his secret affairs with blonde show girls
culprit_and_motive.quote: He had committed murder because the extortionist wanted considerably more money than he had been getting for his continued silence

resolution.value: No legal justice: eleven-year-old Harold, who witnessed the killing and secretly re-hid the corpse in a hollow log off the property, leverages that knowledge to triple his allowance — replacing one blackmailer with another
resolution.quote: All I've done is trade one blackmailer for another, and my own nephew at that!

investigator.value: Harold, the eleven-year-old nephew — first-person narrator, habitual liar, eyewitness and accessory who investigates for his own profit rather than justice
investigator.quote: "I am not in the habit of lying," I lied stiffly.

suspect_architecture.value: Closed household of four: Uncle Walter (the murderer, motive: blackmail over showgirls), Aunt Pearl (ignorant of affair), Elsie the nosy maid (witness only), and narrator Harold (the eleven-year-old observer who becomes the new blackmailer). No mystery of whodunit — the cast exists to isolate Harold as the only possible lurker.
suspect_architecture.quote: Somebody was lurking in the bushes, and it couldn’t possibly have been anyone but you. Elsie and Aunt Pearl were both here in the house.

red_herring.value: The narrator's adult, calculating voice misdirects the reader into assuming Harold is a grown nephew; the withheld fact of his age is the story's planted false impression, sprung at the end.
red_herring.quote: “What are you going to do with that much money? You’re only eleven years old!”

clue_fairness.value: Fairly clued: Harold's physical weakness moving a small body, the two-hour struggle, robe and slippers, being summoned from his room, the 'monthly allowance' set by his uncle, and 'unlike most everyone else of my age' all precede the age reveal.
clue_fairness.quote: I am not particularly strong, and even though the dead man was small and relatively light, it was a physical struggle

social_world.value: Genteel private estate governed by patriarchal family patronage: a pompous lawyer uncle controls money and reputation; the maid surveils; the dependent nephew's only power is the allowance he can extract by threatening exposure to Aunt Pearl or the police.
social_world.quote: He looked like a pompous old lawyer, which is precisely what he was.

alibi.value: Harold falsely claims he was in bed at eleven-forty, then amends to an aimless walk denying he went near the carriage house; the maid Elsie's sighting of him fully dressed at 10:55 breaks the first version, and his own narration confirms both are lies.
alibi.quote: “At eleven-forty? I was in bed, of course.” “You were not,” my uncle said sharply. “Elsie saw you going downstairs at five minutes of eleven

reveal_mechanic.value: Demonstration by the uncle's futile search: Harold proves his leverage not by confessing but by relocating the corpse into a hollow decaying log off the property, so the uncle's failure to find it establishes the hold; the age twist is delivered by the uncle's outburst.
reveal_mechanic.quote: No one venturing into this grove, including my unimaginative uncle, would think of investigating a seemingly solid log.

media_and_audience.value: Crime is entirely private and unpublicised; the only 'audience' invoked is the threatened one — Aunt Pearl and the police — used as leverage rather than as actual investigators.
media_and_audience.quote: I suppose I could find out easily enough what is going on. I could talk to Aunt Pearl, or even to the police. . .

investigator_wound.value: The de facto investigator is the murderer-uncle, whose vulnerability is his tightfisted greed, impulsiveness and secret predilection for showgirls — exactly what both blackmailers exploit; the narrator's own 'wound' is his amoral precocity and habitual lying.
investigator_wound.quote: He also apparently had a predilection for beautiful blonde show girls, about which my Aunt Pearl knew nothing

victims_enemies.value: The dead man is a blackmailer whose only real enemy is his victim, Uncle Walter — a tightfisted lawyer being bled over an affair with show girls, pushed past endurance when the extortionist raised his price.
victims_enemies.quote: He had committed murder because the extortionist wanted considerably more money than he had been getting for his continued silence

suspect_wounds.value: Harold looks guilty of something because he is a compulsive, transparent liar who was indeed sneaking about the grounds at night; his habitual dishonesty and 'downright suspect' behavior make his denials worthless even when they conceal a different crime than his uncle imagines.
suspect_wounds.quote: "To my mind your behavior has always left much to be desired, and has been downright suspect at times."

unreliable_frame.value: Harold narrates and flags his own lies with the repeated tag 'I lied' — a self-declared liar who withholds his age until the final line, letting the reader misjudge him as an adult; Uncle Walter's account is equally evasive about the carriage house.
unreliable_frame.quote: "I am not in the habit of lying," I lied stiffly.

setting_as_constraint.value: A small, closed estate with only four residents plus a nosy maid means any lurker must be Harold by elimination; the grounds' features — oleander bushes, privet hedge, eucalyptus grove, dry creek boundary and hollow log just off the property — dictate both the hasty concealment and the better one.
setting_as_constraint.quote: "Somebody was lurking in the bushes, and it couldn't possibly have been anyone but you. Elsie and Aunt Pearl were both here in the house."

evidence_type.value: Testimonial/eyewitness — the maid Elsie's sighting of Harold going downstairs, plus Harold's own overheard conversation and the muffled gunshot; the body itself is the physical evidence that changes hands.
evidence_type.quote: "Elsie saw you going downstairs at five minutes of eleven, fully dressed; she told me about it when I questioned her this morning."

false_suspect.value: None in the classic sense; Harold is the suspect and is guilty — of body-moving and blackmail, though not of the murder. Aunt Pearl and Elsie are cleared immediately.
false_suspect.quote: "Elsie and Aunt Pearl were both here in the house."

technical_detail.value: Body disposal craft: a decaying eucalyptus-grove log that appears solid but is hollow, off the murderer's property, plus knowledge that eucalyptus bark and leaves peel constantly and make convenient temporary cover.
technical_detail.quote: At first glance it seemed to be solid, but upon careful inspection I discovered that it was for the most part hollow.

moral_ambiguity.value: Uncle Walter is a pompous but cornered man driven to impulsive murder by an extortionist's escalating demands; Harold, an eleven-year-old, is not evil so much as precociously amoral — treating blackmail as a career choice rather than a crime.
moral_ambiguity.quote: "All I've done is trade one blackmailer for another, and my own nephew at that!"
